claim: Phage-derived peptidoglycan hydrolases (lysins) are considered promising alternatives to conventional antibiotics due to their direct peptidoglycan degradation activity and low risk of resistance development.
source: Phage-derived peptidoglycan hydrolases (i.e. lysins) are considered promising alternatives to conventional antibiotics due to their direct peptidoglycan degradation activity and low risk of resistance development.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific consensus about lysins as antibiotic alternatives.

claim: The discovery of lysins is often hampered by the limited availability of phage genomes.
source: The discovery of these enzymes is often hampered by the limited availability of phage genomes.
evidence: This is a general statement about limitations in the field, representing established knowledge.

claim: Five peptidoglycan hydrolases from the Acinetobacter baumannii proteome (PHAb7-PHAb11) were identified using PlyF307 lysin-derived peptide as a template.
source: As a proof-of-concept, five peptidoglycan hydrolases from the Acinetobacter baumannii proteome (PHAb7-PHAb11) were identified using PlyF307 lysin-derived peptide as a template.
evidence: This describes the experimental approach and results of the study.

claim: PHAb10 and PHAb11 showed potent bactericidal activity against multiple pathogens even after treatment at 100°C for 1 hr.
source: Among them, PHAb10 and PHAb11 showed potent bactericidal activity against multiple pathogens even after treatment at 100°C for 1 hr, while the other three were thermosensitive.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing bactericidal activity after heat treatment.

claim: PHAb7, PHAb8, and PHAb9 were thermosensitive.
source: Among them, PHAb10 and PHAb11 showed potent bactericidal activity against multiple pathogens even after treatment at 100°C for 1 hr, while the other three were thermosensitive.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing loss of activity after heat treatment.

claim: Crystal structures of PHAb8, PHAb10, and PHAb11 were solved.
source: We solved the crystal structures of PHAb8, PHAb10, and PHAb11 and unveiled that hyper-thermostable PHAb10 underwent a unique folding-refolding thermodynamic scheme mediated by a dimer-monomer transition, while thermosensitive PHAb8 formed a monomer.
evidence: This is supported by crystallographic data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Hyper-thermostable PHAb10 underwent a unique folding-refolding thermodynamic scheme mediated by a dimer-monomer transition.
source: We solved the crystal structures of PHAb8, PHAb10, and PHAb11 and unveiled that hyper-thermostable PHAb10 underwent a unique folding-refolding thermodynamic scheme mediated by a dimer-monomer transition, while thermosensitive PHAb8 formed a monomer.
evidence: This is supported by structural and biochemical data showing dimer-monomer transitions.

claim: Thermosensitive PHAb8 formed a monomer.
source: We solved the crystal structures of PHAb8, PHAb10, and PHAb11 and unveiled that hyper-thermostable PHAb10 underwent a unique folding-refolding thermodynamic scheme mediated by a dimer-monomer transition, while thermosensitive PHAb8 formed a monomer.
evidence: This is supported by crystallographic data showing monomeric structure.

claim: Two mouse models of bacterial infection demonstrated the safety and efficacy of PHAb10.
source: Two mouse models of bacterial infection further demonstrated the safety and efficacy of PHAb10.
evidence: This is supported by in vivo experimental data from mouse infection models.

claim: Antimicrobial resistance remains a growing global threat.
source: Despite decades of concerted action from all over the world, antimicrobial resistance remains a growing global threat today (Nathan, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Nathan, 2020.

claim: The misuse and overuse of antimicrobials leads to their accumulation in the environment, eventually increasing the chances of bacterial pathogens to acquire resistance.
source: The misuse and overuse of antimicrobials leads to their accumulation in the environment, eventually increasing the chances of bacterial pathogens to acquire resistance (Van Boeckel et al., 2019; Rawson et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Van Boeckel et al., 2019 and Rawson et al., 2020.

claim: The concept of 'One Health' has been proposed to address the alarming levels of antimicrobial resistance.
source: Therefore, the concept of 'One Health' has been proposed to address the alarming levels of antimicrobial resistance (McEwen and Collignon, 2018; Hernando-Amado et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to McEwen and Collignon, 2018 and Hernando-Amado et al., 2019.

claim: The number of bacteria resistant to first-line drugs, as well as second- and third-line drugs, has been increasing in recent decades.
source: In recent decades, the number of bacteria resistant to first-line drugs, as well as second- and third-line drugs, has been increasing.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about antimicrobial resistance trends.

claim: Some bacteria have been identified as multidrug-resistant, extensively drug-resistant, or pan-drug-resistant isolates.
source: Some of these bacteria have even been identified as multidrug-resistant, extensively drug-resistant, or pan-drug-resistant isolates (Talaat et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Talaat et al., 2022.

claim: Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus, vancomycin-resistant S. aureus, vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus, colistin-resistant Enterobacteriaceae, third-generation cephalosporin-resistant Escherichia coli and Klebsiella pneumoniae, carbapenem-resistant E. coli, K. pneumoniae, and Pseudomonas aeruginosa, and multidrug-resistant Acinetobacter baumannii pose a serious threat and are the leading cause of morbidity and mortality in human infectious diseases.
source: For example, methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus, vancomycin-resistant S. aureus, vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus, colistin-resistant Enterobacteriaceae, third-generation cephalosporin-resistant Escherichia coli and Klebsiella pneumoniae, carbapenem-resistant E. coli, K. pneumoniae, and Pseudomonas aeruginosa, and multidrug-resistant Acinetobacter baumannii pose a serious threat and are the leading cause of morbidity and mortality in human infectious diseases (Brink, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Brink, 2019.

claim: The global medical need for new antimicrobials has not yet been fully addressed.
source: In addition, the global medical need for new antimicrobials has not yet been fully addressed.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of antimicrobial development.

claim: Bacterial peptidoglycan is a promising target for the development of antimicrobial agents with a low risk of resistance development.
source: Considerable evidence shows that bacterial peptidoglycan is a promising target for the development of antimicrobial agents with a low risk of resistance development.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge in the field.

claim: Lysins have been shown to be efficient alternatives to traditional antibiotics for infections caused by Gram-positive bacteria in various animal models.
source: In recent years, lysins have been shown to be efficient alternatives to traditional antibiotics for infections caused by Gram-positive bacteria in various animal models (De Maesschalck et al., 2020; Schmelcher and Loessner, 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to De Maesschalck et al., 2020 and Schmelcher and Loessner, 2021.

claim: Several lysins targeting S. aureus have been evaluated in clinical trials.
source: Encouragingly, several lysins targeting S. aureus have been evaluated in clinical trials (Theuretzbacher and Piddock, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Theuretzbacher and Piddock, 2019.

claim: The development of lysins targeting Gram-negative bacteria is relatively recent, mainly because the bacterial outer membrane prevents lysins from accessing their peptidoglycan substrates.
source: However, the development of lysins targeting Gram-negative bacteria is relatively recent, mainly because the bacterial outer membrane prevents lysins from accessing their peptidoglycan substrates.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about the challenges in developing lysins for Gram-negative bacteria.

claim: Artilysins are constructed by fusion of cationic nonapeptides to effectively eradicate resistant and persistent A. baumannii.
source: For instance, Artilysins are constructed by fusion of cationic nonapeptides to effectively eradicate resistant and persistent A. baumannii (Defraine et al., 2016)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Defraine et al., 2016.

claim: Innolysins are engineered by fusion of receptor-binding proteins to display bactericidal activity against E. coli that was resistant to third-generation cephalosporins.
source: Innolysins are engineered by fusion of receptor-binding proteins to display bactericidal activity against E. coli that was resistant to third-generation cephalosporins (Zampara et al., 2020)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Zampara et al., 2020.

claim: Lysocins are bioengineered lysin-bacteriocin fusion molecules that are able to deliver lysin across the outer membrane of Gram-negative bacteria and show selective anti-Pseudomonal activity.
source: bioengineered lysin-bacteriocin fusion molecule, i.e., Lysocins, are able to deliver lysin across the outer membrane of Gram-negative bacteria and show selective anti-Pseudomonal activity (Heselpoth et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Heselpoth et al., 2019.

claim: The VersaTile-driven platform can rapidly screen engineered lysins active against A. baumannii from tens of thousands of combinations by integrating new DNA assembly methods and iterative screening procedures.
source: In addition, the establishment of high-throughput mining or engineering strategies has accelerated the discovery of active lysins against Gram-negative pathogens, e.g., the VersaTile-driven platform, which can rapidly screen engineered lysins active against A. baumannii from tens of thousands of combinations by integrating new DNA assembly methods and iterative screening procedures (Gerstmans et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Gerstmans et al., 2020.

claim: The discovery of lysins against Gram-negative bacteria that meet the needs described in the WHO priority pathogen list is still urgently needed.
source: However, compared with the current progress in the clinical translation of lysins against Gram-positive bacteria, the discovery of lysins against Gram-negative bacteria that meet the needs described in the WHO priority pathogen list is still urgently needed (Briers and Lavigne, 2015; Lai et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Briers and Lavigne, 2015 and Lai et al., 2020.

claim: The discovery of phage-derived peptidoglycan hydrolases has been hampered by limited sources of published phage genome data.
source: Additionally, the discovery of phage-derived peptidoglycan hydrolases has also been hampered by limited sources of published phage genome data.
evidence: This is a statement about limitations in the field.

claim: Recent progress in lysins targeting Gram-negative bacteria have demonstrated a clue linking antibacterial activity to their internal antimicrobial peptides.
source: Although not yet tested extensively, recent progress in lysins targeting Gram-negative bacteria have demonstrated a clue linking antibacterial activity to their internal antimicrobial peptides (Vázquez et al., 2021)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Vázquez et al., 2021.

claim: Lysins cross the bacterial outer membrane and contact its underlying peptidoglycan substrates via antimicrobial peptides.
source: by which lysins cross the bacterial outer membrane and contact its underlying peptidoglycan substrates (Lood et al., 2015; Thandar et al., 2016; Li et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Lood et al., 2015, Thandar et al., 2016, and Li et al., 2021.

claim: The antimicrobial peptide P307 was derived from PlyF307 lysin.
source: As a proof-of-concept, we here used the antimicrobial peptide P307 derived from PlyF307 lysin (Lood et al., 2015) as a template to search for peptidoglycan hydrolases from the A. baumannii proteome database
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Lood et al., 2015.

claim: 204 hits were identified from the A. baumannii proteome database using P307 as a template.
source: Finally, 204 hits were identified and further divided into five clades based on phylogenetic analysis.
evidence: This describes the results of the screening approach.

claim: The 204 hits were divided into five clades based on phylogenetic analysis.
source: Finally, 204 hits were identified and further divided into five clades based on phylogenetic analysis.
evidence: This describes the phylogenetic analysis performed on the hits.

claim: Clade I contained 162 hits with high similarity (>85%) to the AcLys lysin from A. baumannii 5057UW prophage.
source: Clade I contained 162 hits with high similarity (>85%) to the AcLys lysin from A. baumannii 5057UW prophage (Figure 1b)
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis data shown in Figure 1b.

claim: Clades II–V contained 42 hits with relatively lower homology (40–77%) to each other.
source: and clade II–V contained 42 hits with relatively lower homology (40–77%) to each other (Figure 1b; Figure 1—figure supplement 2a).
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis data shown in Figure 1b and Figure 1—figure supplement 2a.

claim: All five PHAbs were well expressed as soluble proteins in E. coli BL21(DE3) with high purity.
source: As expected, all five PHAbs were well expressed as soluble proteins in E. coli BL21(DE3) with high purity (Figure 2—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is supported by SDS-PAGE data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1a.

claim: All PHAbs form clear zones on the autoclaved A. baumannii lawns even at a low concentration of 2.5 μg/ml.
source: The results showed that all PHAbs form clear zones on the autoclaved A. baumannii lawns even at a low concentration of 2.5 μg/ml (Figure 2—figure supplement 1b)
evidence: This is supported by halo assay data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1b.

claim: PHAb10 and PHAb11 showed larger size of clear zones under each concentration tested compared to other PHAbs.
source: Among these PHAbs, PHAb10 and PHAb11 showed larger size of clear zones under each concentration tested (Figure 2a)
evidence: This is supported by halo assay data shown in Figure 2a.

claim: PHAb10 and PHAb11 exhibited outstanding bactericidal activity against all strains tested, with a 3.5–4.6 log reduction in viable bacterial counts after treatment for 1 hr with 50 μg/ml of each enzyme.
source: Consistent with the halo assay, PHAb10 and PHAb11 exhibited outstanding bactericidal activity against all strains tested, with a 3.5–4.6 log reduction in viable bacterial counts after treatment for 1 hr with 50 μg/ml of each enzyme (Figure 2b).
evidence: This is supported by log-killing assay data shown in Figure 2b.

claim: The potent bactericidal activity of PHAb10 and PHAb11 was time-dependent.
source: Like other lysins, the potent bactericidal activity of PHAb10 and PHAb11 was time-dependent.
evidence: This is supported by time-killing curve data.

claim: After treatment with 50 μg/ml of PHAb10, a ∼0.9 log reduction in viable A. baumannii 3437 was observed within the first 30 s, with a substantial reduction to 3.1 logs after 15 min.
source: After treatment with 50 μg/ml of either enzyme, a ∼0.9 log reduction in viable A. baumannii 3437 for both enzymes were observed within the first 30 s, with a substantial reduction to 3.1 logs (from 6.0 log to 2.9 log) for PHAb10 and 2.5 logs (from 6.0 log to 3.5 log) for PHAb11 after 15 min (Figure 2c).
evidence: This is supported by time-killing curve data shown in Figure 2c.

claim: After treatment with 50 μg/ml of PHAb11, a ∼0.9 log reduction in viable A. baumannii 3437 was observed within the first 30 s, with a substantial reduction to 2.5 logs after 15 min.
source: After treatment with 50 μg/ml of either enzyme, a ∼0.9 log reduction in viable A. baumannii 3437 for both enzymes were observed within the first 30 s, with a substantial reduction to 3.1 logs (from 6.0 log to 2.9 log) for PHAb10 and 2.5 logs (from 6.0 log to 3.5 log) for PHAb11 after 15 min (Figure 2c).
evidence: This is supported by time-killing curve data shown in Figure 2c.

claim: Robust bactericidal activity was observed for PHAb10 and PHAb11 in exponential and stationary phase cultures of A. baumannii, P. aeruginosa, E. coli, K. pneumoniae, Streptococcus suis, and E. faecalis.
source: Interestingly, robust bactericidal activity was observed for both enzymes in exponential and stationary phase cultures of A. baumannii, P. aeruginosa, E. coli, K. pneumoniae, Streptococcus suis, and E. faecalis (Figure 2d).
evidence: This is supported by log-killing assay data shown in Figure 2d.

claim: Exponential bacteria were more susceptible to PHAb10 and PHAb11 than stationary bacteria.
source: It should also be noted that exponential bacteria were more susceptible to these two enzymes than stationary bacteria, similar to observations reported elsewhere (Lood et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and a citation to Lood et al., 2015.

claim: For S. aureus, detectable susceptibility to PHAb11 was only observed in its exponential phase.
source: However, for S. aureus, detectable susceptibility to PHAb11 was only observed in its exponential phase (Figure 2d).
evidence: This is supported by log-killing assay data shown in Figure 2d.

claim: PHAb10 and PHAb11 exhibited dose-dependent killing against sensitive Gram-negative and Gram-positive strains tested.
source: In addition, PHAb10 and PHAb11 exhibited dose-dependent killing against sensitive Gram-negative and Gram-positive strains tested.
evidence: This is supported by dose-response experimental data.

claim: Treatment with 6.25 μg/ml PHAb10 for 1 hr resulted in a ∼3 log reduction in A. baumannii, a ∼2.7 log reduction in P. aeruginosa, a ∼3 log reduction in E. coli, a ∼1.08 log reduction in K. pneumoniae, and a ∼0.94 log reduction in S. suis.
source: Specifically, treatment with 6.25 μg/ml PHAb10 for 1 hr resulted in a ∼3 log reduction in A. baumannii, a ∼2.7 log reduction in P. aeruginosa, a ∼3 log reduction in E. coli, a ∼1.08 log reduction in K. pneumoniae, and a ∼0.94 log reduction in S. suis
evidence: This is supported by dose-response experimental data.

claim: Treatment with 6.25 μg/ml PHAb11 for 1 hr caused a ∼2.8 log reduction in A. baumannii, a ∼2.6 log reduction in P. aeruginosa, a ∼2.7 log reduction in E. coli, a ∼0.69 log reduction in K. pneumoniae, a ∼1.3 log reduction in S. aureus, and a ∼2.15 log reduction in S. suis.
source: and treatment with 6.25 μg/ml PHAb11 for 1 hr caused a ∼2.8 log reduction in A. baumannii, a ∼2.6 log reduction in P. aeruginosa, a ∼2.7 log reduction in E. coli, a ∼0.69 log reduction in K. pneumoniae, a ∼1.3 log reduction in S. aureus, and a ∼2.15 log reduction in S. suis (Figure 2e).
evidence: This is supported by dose-response experimental data shown in Figure 2e.

claim: E. faecalis was more sensitive to PHAb10 and PHAb11, showing a ∼3.8 log and a ∼4.6 log reduction respectively after treatment with 10 μg/ml of each enzyme for 1 hr.
source: Interestingly, E. faecalis was more sensitive to PHAb10 and PHAb11, showing a ∼3.8 log and a ∼4.6 log reduction respectively after treatment with 10 μg/ml of each enzyme for 1 hr (Figure 2f).
evidence: This is supported by log-killing assay data shown in Figure 2f.

claim: All tested strains, whether antibiotic-resistant or not, were sensitive to PHAb10 and PHAb11.
source: Our results showed that all tested strains, whether antibiotic-resistant or not, were sensitive to PHAb10 and PHAb11 (Figure 2g and h).
evidence: This is supported by log-killing assay data shown in Figure 2g and h.

claim: Gram-negative bacteria were more sensitive to PHAb10, with 3.9–6.0 log reductions for A. baumannii isolates, 3.7–5.0 log reductions for E. coli isolates, 2.4–4.3 log reductions for P. aeruginosa isolates, and 1.1–3.6 log reductions for K. pneumoniae isolates.
source: Importantly, Gram-negative bacteria were more sensitive to PHAb10, with 3.9–6.0 log reductions for A. baumannii isolates, 3.7–5.0 log reductions for E. coli isolates, 2.4–4.3 log reductions for P. aeruginosa isolates, and 1.1–3.6 log reductions for K. pneumoniae isolates (Figure 2g).
evidence: This is supported by log-killing assay data shown in Figure 2g.

claim: PHAb11 was more bactericidal than PHAb10 against Gram-positive bacteria, causing 1.8–4.3 log reductions for S. aureus isolates, 4.5–5.0 log reductions for E. faecalis isolates, and 1.0–6.1 log reductions for various streptococcal strains.
source: In contrast, PHAb11 was more bactericidal than PHAb10 against Gram-positive bacteria, causing 1.8–4.3 log reductions for S. aureus isolates, 4.5–5.0 log reductions for E. faecalis isolates, and 1.0–6.1 log reductions for various streptococcal strains (Figure 2h).
evidence: This is supported by log-killing assay data shown in Figure 2h.

claim: PHAb10 and PHAb11 remained highly active at pH 5.0–10.0, and the maximum bactericidal activity was observed at pH 7.0 for both enzymes.
source: Further biochemical characterization showed that PHAb10 and PHAb11 remained highly active at pH 5.0–10.0, and the maximum bactericidal activity was observed at pH 7.0 for both enzymes (Figure 2—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: This is supported by pH stability assay data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1c.

claim: PHAb10 and PHAb11 were sensitive to NaCl and urea in a dose-dependent inhibitory manner.
source: Similar to other previously reported lysins (Larpin et al., 2018; Kim et al., 2020), PHAb10 and PHAb11 were sensitive to NaCl and urea in a dose-dependent inhibitory manner (Figure 2—figure supplement 1d).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1d and citations to Larpin et al., 2018 and Kim et al., 2020.

claim: PHAb10 and PHAb11 retained outstanding bactericidal activity after heat treatment at temperature up to 100°C for 1 hr.
source: Surprisingly, both enzymes retained outstanding bactericidal activity after heat treatment at temperature up to 100°C for 1 hr (Figure 2i).
evidence: This is supported by thermostability assay data shown in Figure 2i.

claim: After 1 hr treatment at 100°C, the bactericidal activity was improved slightly for both PHAb10 and PHAb11.
source: Indeed, after 1 hr treatment at 100°C, the bactericidal activity was improved slightly for both enzymes.
evidence: This is supported by thermostability assay data.

claim: PHAb7, PHAb8, and PHAb9 completely lost their activity after treatment at 70°C for 1 hr.
source: In contrast, PHAb7, PHAb8, and PHAb9 completely lost their activity after treatment at 70°C for 1 hr (Figure 2—figure supplement 1e).
evidence: This is supported by thermostability assay data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1e.

claim: PHAb10 contains a putative lysozyme catalytic domain (amino acids 1–110, P10-Lys) and a C-terminal cationic peptide (amino acids 111–149, P10-CP).
source: Structural prediction analysis showed that PHAb10 contains a putative lysozyme catalytic domain (amino acids 1–110, P10-Lys) and a C-terminal cationic peptide (amino acids 111–149, P10-CP)
evidence: This is based on structural prediction analysis.

claim: PHAb11 contains an N-terminal cationic peptide with unknown function (amino acids 1–36, P11-NP), followed by a putative lysozyme catalytic domain (amino acids 37–145, P11-Lys, with 68.5% sequence similarity with P10-Lys) and a C-terminal cationic peptide (amino acids 146–184, P11-CP, which shows 94.9% sequence similarity with P10-CP).
source: whereas PHAb11 contains an N-terminal cationic peptide with unknown function (amino acids 1–36, P11-NP), followed by a putative lysozyme catalytic domain (amino acids 37–145, P11-Lys, with 68.5% sequence similarity with P10-Lys) and a C-terminal cationic peptide (amino acids 146–184, P11-CP, which shows 94.9% sequence similarity with P10-CP) (Figure 3a).
evidence: This is based on structural prediction analysis shown in Figure 3a.

claim: The cationic region of phage lysins can facilitate their penetration into the outer membrane, thereby fulfilling their bactericidal activity against Gram-negative bacteria.
source: Studies have shown that the cationic region of phage lysins can facilitate their penetration into the outer membrane, thereby fulfilling their bactericidal activity against Gram-negative bacteria (Lood et al., 2015; Larpin et al., 2018; Li et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Lood et al., 2015, Larpin et al., 2018, and Li et al., 2021.

claim: P10-CP, P11-CP, and P11-NP might act as antimicrobial peptides based on in silico analysis.
source: To examine whether it is the reason for the killing ability of PHAb10 and PHAb11 against Gram-negative bacteria, we further analyzed in silico the physicochemical properties of these putative cationic peptides harbored by these two enzymes and found that all three peptides, i.e., P10-CP, P11-CP, and P11-NP might act as antimicrobial peptides (Supplementary file 1a).
evidence: This is based on in silico analysis of physicochemical properties.

claim: Bactericidal activity was observed in P10-CP and P11-CP against A. baumannii, P. aeruginosa, S. aureus, and E. faecalis in both the exponential and stationary phases.
source: As shown in Figure 3b, we observed bactericidal activity in P10-CP and P11-CP against A. baumannii, P. aeruginosa, S. aureus, and E. faecalis in both the exponential and stationary phases.
evidence: This is supported by log-killing assay data shown in Figure 3b.

claim: Rare lytic activity was observed in P11-NP.
source: However, rare lytic activity was observed in P11-NP, suggesting that its function remains to be established.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data.

claim: P11-CP was more robust than P10-CP.
source: Notably, P11-CP was more robust than P10-CP (Figure 3b), which might be due to the presence of an additional positively charged amino acid (i.e. lysine) in P11-CP (Supplementary file 1a).
evidence: This is supported by log-killing assay data shown in Figure 3b and sequence analysis.

claim: The putative lysozyme catalytic domains of two enzymes, P10-Lys, P11-Lys, and P11-N showed rare bactericidal activity against all Gram-negative and Gram-positive bacteria tested.
source: More importantly, the putative lysozyme catalytic domains of two enzymes, P10-Lys, P11-Lys, and P11-N showed rare bactericidal activity against all Gram-negative and Gram-positive bacteria tested (Figure 3c and d)
evidence: This is supported by log-killing assay data shown in Figure 3c and d.

claim: The antimicrobial peptides P10-CP and P11-CP were essential for the bactericidal activity of PHAb10 and PHAb11.
source: which indicated that the antimicrobial peptides, namely P10-CP and P11-CP, were essential for the bactericidal activity of both enzymes.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing that lysozyme domains alone have no activity.

claim: P11-C showed higher bactericidal activity than the holoenzyme PHAb11 against all bacteria tested.
source: Curiously, for unknown reasons, P11-C showed higher bactericidal activity than the holoenzyme PHAb11 against all bacteria tested (Figure 3d).
evidence: This is supported by log-killing assay data shown in Figure 3d.

claim: Lysozyme-containing truncations from PHAb10 and PHAb11 showed hydrolytic activity only toward peptidoglycan from Gram-negative bacteria but not from Gram-positive bacteria.
source: Results showed that lysozyme-containing truncations from both enzymes showed hydrolytic activity only toward peptidoglycan from Gram-negative bacteria but not from Gram-positive bacteria (Figure 3e)
evidence: This is supported by halo assay data shown in Figure 3e.

claim: The killing of Gram-positive bacteria by PHAb10 and PHAb11 is probably mediated mainly by their internal antimicrobial peptides, i.e., P10-CP and P11-CP.
source: suggesting that the killing of Gram-positive bacteria by PHAb10 and PHAb11 is probably mediated mainly by their internal antimicrobial peptides, i.e., P10-CP and P11-CP.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing no peptidoglycan hydrolytic activity against Gram-positive bacteria.

claim: Rare peptidoglycan hydrolytic activity was observed in P10-CP and P11-CP.
source: Supporting to this assumption, rare peptidoglycan hydrolytic activity was observed in P10-CP and P11-CP (Figure 3e).
evidence: This is supported by halo assay data shown in Figure 3e.

claim: The killing of Gram-negative bacteria by PHAb10 and PHAb11 might be a combination of lysozyme-mediated peptidoglycan hydrolytic activity and antimicrobial peptide-mediated outer membrane-disruption activity.
source: Altogether, these results suggested that the killing of Gram-negative bacteria by PHAb10 and PHAb11 might be a combination of lysozyme-mediated peptidoglycan hydrolytic activity and antimicrobial peptide-mediated outer membrane-disruption activity.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing both peptidoglycan hydrolytic activity and antimicrobial peptide activity.

claim: PHAb8 was a monomer.
source: Results showed that PHAb8 was a monomer (Figure 4a; Figure 4—figure supplement 1a)
evidence: This is supported by crystal structure data shown in Figure 4a and Figure 4—figure supplement 1a.

claim: PHAb10 formed an asymmetric dimer.
source: while PHAb10 (Figure 4b) and PHAb11 (Figure 4c) formed an asymmetric dimer.
evidence: This is supported by crystal structure data shown in Figure 4b.

claim: PHAb11 formed an asymmetric dimer.
source: while PHAb10 (Figure 4b) and PHAb11 (Figure 4c) formed an asymmetric dimer.
evidence: This is supported by crystal structure data shown in Figure 4c.

claim: The two asymmetric units of PHAb10 formed an antiparallel dimer with a rotation angle of 177.2° along the rotation axis and a distance of 10.5 Å between them.
source: Specifically, the two asymmetric units of PHAb10 formed an antiparallel dimer with a rotation angle of 177.2° along the rotation axis and a distance of 10.5 Å between them.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis of the crystal structure.

claim: PHAb10 dimer adopted a circularly permuted architecture, in which the N-terminus of one chain and the C-terminus of another chain formed a cavity, which might be the binding site of the peptidoglycan substrate.
source: Further, PHAb10 dimer adopted a circularly permuted architecture, in which the N-terminus of one chain and the C-terminus of another chain formed a cavity, which might be the binding site of the peptidoglycan substrate (Figure 4b).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis of the crystal structure shown in Figure 4b.

claim: The two subunits of PHAb11 formed a tail-to-tail dimer with a rotation angle of –179.4° along the rotation axis and a distance of 37.1 Å between them.
source: The two subunits of PHAb11 formed a tail-to-tail dimer with a rotation angle of –179.4° along the rotation axis and a distance of 37.1 Å between them.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis of the crystal structure.

claim: Each PHAb11 monomer contained an independent substrate-binding cavity around its catalytic triad.
source: Each PHAb11 monomer contained an independent substrate-binding cavity around its catalytic triad (Figure 4c).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis of the crystal structure shown in Figure 4c.

claim: The N-terminal 36 amino acids, P11-NP, were missing in the PHAb11 dimer crystal structure.
source: Notably, the N-terminal 36 amino acids, P11-NP, were missing in our PHAb11 dimer.
evidence: This is an observation from the crystal structure.

claim: P11-NP may be destroyed during crystal formation.
source: We speculated that it may be destroyed during crystal formation.
evidence: This is speculation based on the missing density in the crystal structure.

claim: PHAb8 showed high topological similarity to monomeric PHAb10 and PHAb11, with the typical catalytic triad (Glu-Asp-Thr) located at the coil region.
source: Interestingly, PHAb8 showed high topological similarity to monomeric PHAb10 and PHAb11, with the typical catalytic triad (Glu-Asp-Thr) located at the coil region (Figure 4d; Figure 4—figure supplement 1a–c).
evidence: This is based on structural comparison shown in Figure 4d and Figure 4—figure supplement 1a–c.

claim: The catalytic triad of PHAb8, PHAb10, and PHAb11 were highly conserved in homologous proteins, including AcLys (PDB ID 6ET6), LysF1 (PDB ID 7M5I), SpmX-Mur-Ae (PDB ID 6H9D), P22 (PDB ID 2ANX), and R21 (PDB ID 3HDE).

claim: PHAb8, PHAb10, and PHAb11 superimposed well with T4 lysozyme, especially in their Glu-Asp-Thr catalytic triad regions.

claim: PHAb8, PHAb10, and PHAb11 may be phage-originated.

claim: PHAb8, PHAb10, and PHAb11 were highly evolutionarily related to T4 lysozyme and might share similar catalytic mechanisms of action.
source: All these observations together indicated that PHAb8, PHAb10, and PHAb11 were highly evolutionarily related to T4 lysozyme and might share similar catalytic mechanisms of action.
evidence: This is inferred from structural similarity and phylogenetic analysis.

We found significantly less viable bacteria remaining at the site of infection compared to Tris-treated controls (Figure 6b).
